units.text: Trace the orange path from internet requests into the ingress VPC. An internet-facing Application Load Balancer provides the shared entry point and spans multiple Availability Zones.
Follow the path through Transit Gateway to the application VPCs. Register reachable, supported private IP targets; instance identifiers cannot register targets across VPCs.
The three lower panels connect centralized TLS and WAF controls with target health checks, forward and return routes, and security groups and network access lists.
With the full architecture visible, separate a shared entry point from proven application reachability. Centralized policy succeeds only when requests and responses can traverse the complete path.
Start with the two spoke VPCs on the left. Their private workloads send internet-bound traffic through Transit Gateway toward the centralized egress VPC.
Inside the egress VPC, trace traffic from the Transit Gateway attachment through the public NAT gateway and internet gateway. Responses must return to the originating spoke.
Read the three lower panels together: configure default routes toward egress, add return routes for spoke address ranges, and compare Availability Zone resilience with processing costs.
The complete slide highlights a deliberate tradeoff. Centralized NAT can consolidate egress, but it requires correct return routing and does not provide deep packet inspection.
Compare the two central diagrams. On the left, request and response cross the same firewall endpoint or appliance, allowing it to track the connection state.
On the right, the response bypasses inspection or uses a different endpoint. An allow rule cannot restore connection state that the returning traffic never reaches.

The lower panels show the inspection VPC pattern: route through firewall endpoints, enable appliance mode on the Transit Gateway inspection attachment, and verify both directions and Availability Zone paths.
Return to the complete comparison. A native Transit Gateway attached Network Firewall offers managed symmetry, while a dedicated inspection VPC remains another deployment option.
Follow traffic from the workload to the Gateway Load Balancer endpoint. The endpoint is the route table target that inserts inspection into the traffic path.
The Gateway Load Balancer distributes flows to healthy appliances. The highlighted packet uses GENEVE encapsulation on UDP port sixty eighty-one while preserving the original packet for inspection.
Trace the inspection round trip back through the load balancer and endpoint. VPC routing then forwards the packet; forward and return traffic must preserve the required symmetry.

With the full slide visible, distinguish traffic steering from inspection. Gateway Load Balancer distributes network flows, while the appliances perform the inspection and require their own health and capacity planning.
Compare the deployment panels. The left places firewall endpoints in dedicated VPC subnets, supporting distributed deployments or a centralized inspection VPC.

The right attaches Network Firewall directly to Transit Gateway through a managed network function attachment. This model manages the attachment across Availability Zones and preserves traffic symmetry.
Read the lower-left policy sequence. Stateless rules run first and can drop, pass, or forward traffic to stateful inspection; flow and alert logs help validate the configured behavior.
The complete slide connects policy with placement. Route traffic through the chosen firewall path; native Transit Gateway attachments use static routes and have appliance mode enabled automatically.
